content.text:
can you take a look, we are using git-sync as part of our mirror pipeline: 

The GitHub mirror workers in us-east-2 are at their 20-pod maximum. A handful of very large repos are being synced 2–4× more often than this morning, and the queue is growing faster than 20 workers can clear it. The "large first-time clone" theory from the alert bot (marvin) is wrong: first-time clones are flat at about 15 per hour all day.

What's driving it (repos with the most total sync work, 14:00–15:15Z vs 17:00Z–now)

Each of these syncs re-checks 20–65k refs to change about one. Total incoming jobs barely moved (about 9–10k an hour since 15:00Z); the problem is that more of them are these slow ones. That's why the slowest-5% sync time tripled from 5s to 16s. "Target already being synced, deferred" log lines went from 181 an hour at 10:00Z to 1,351 at 17:00Z, so the same repos keep getting new jobs while a sync of them is still running.

I found why each of these syncs costs the same whether 1 ref changed or 50k did. I couldn't confirm what started the 2–4× increase at around 17:00Z.

**Every sync re-checks the whole repo, by design.** A sync job (`pkg/gitjobs/jobs.go:105`) names only the source and target, not the ref that changed. So each webhook runs a full comparison, and in git-sync that costs time proportional to the total number of refs:

1. **Listing the GitHub refs.** The worker asks for all refs (`AllRefs: true`, `mirror-pipeline/cmd/worker/syncer.go:832`), which makes git-sync request everything under `refs/` (`internal/planner/types.go:248`). That includes `refs/pull/*`, which the worker only drops after the list arrives. On busy repos the PR refs can outnumber the branches, so GitHub may be sending well over the 20–65k refs that get compared.
2. **Listing the mirror's refs.** git-sync fetches the target's complete ref list (`internal/syncer/syncer.go:918`). The protocol version it uses for this has no way to ask for less.
3. **Fetching from GitHub.** The fetch sends one line for the changed ref plus a "have" line for every ref tip already on the mirror (`internal/gitproto/fetch.go:251` and `:272`). That's tens of thousands of lines, about 3 MB of request body for 65k refs, and GitHub has to check every one before it sends back a tiny pack. When one ref is being updated, its old value on the mirror is enough.

So more of these syncs means p95 goes up, even though the total job count barely moved.

**Repeat jobs.** I couldn't find the "Target already being synced, deferred" log line in my local `mirror-pipeline` checkout or in entiredb, so the deployed code may differ. Since every sync reconciles the whole repo, a job that arrives during a running sync of the same target needs no work beyond one follow-up sync. If deferral puts each job back in the queue instead of merging them, 10 webhooks during one slow sync become 10 more full syncs later. A rise from 181 to 1,351 deferrals an hour fits that. A busy repo can then stay at full-repo cost almost continuously.

**What I'd do, cheapest first:**
- **Now, in the worker:** keep at most one pending sync per target and drop the rest. Nothing is lost, because the next sync picks up every change. This is the most likely way to bring the queue back down.
- **git-sync:** when only a few refs are being created or updated, send far fewer "haves": the old value of each updated ref plus the default branch tip. This cuts the 3 MB request and the matching work on GitHub's side. It's a small change in `fetchPackV2` and its callers.
- **git-sync and worker:** avoid listing `refs/pull/*` from GitHub. The listing can't exclude a namespace, only include prefixes. So this means listing named namespaces instead of `refs/`, which conflicts with the empty-source safety check that requires the full listing. That needs a design decision.
- **Later:** put the changed refs in the job and let git-sync list only those (narrowing the GitHub side by exact ref name). The mirror's full ref list would still be fetched each time, but that request stays inside our own servers.

**Still open:** why these repos jumped 2–4× at 17:00Z. Possibilities include a merge-queue or CI bot pushing more often, the re-kicker, or retries after "raced" outcomes. Grouping the incoming webhooks for the top repos by event type and sender would show which. I can query Datadog for that, or write the `fetchPackV2` change. Which would help most?

# One mirror sync per target at a time, through a KV lease

Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Accepted
Relates to: [entiredb ADR `20260521-mirror-bootstrap-on-create.md`](https://github.com/entirehq/entiredb/blob/main/docs/adrs/20260521-mirror-bootstrap-on-create.md),
[`mirror-sync-failure-index.md`](mirror-sync-failure-index.md)

## Context

Mirror workers pull sync jobs from one durable per placement and kind. Nothing
stops two workers from syncing the same target at once. The 1 s publish dedup
window only collapses retries of one publish.

On 2026-10-15 a new private 7 GB GitHub mirror took about 3.5 minutes to
bootstrap. Two GitHub pushes arrived during that time. Fanout published a job
for each. Other workers saw an empty target, because a one-shot bootstrap
writes no ref until it ends, and started two more full bootstraps. Each loser
failed on `refs/heads/dev: already exists` after its pack was committed. That
left about 63 GB of duplicate packs, and concurrent indexing took nodes to
61 of 61.9 GB.

The same race happens on small repos all the time: 39k raced syncs and 33k
leaked packs in the 15 days to 2026-10-15.

## Decision

A worker holds a lease on the target repo while it syncs. A job that finds the
lease held writes a pending note to a durable bucket and acks. The holder
republishes the notes as fresh jobs when it finishes. The rekicker republishes
notes that no holder handled.
Pending work is as durable as any other job. A deferred push stays in
`mirror_sync_pending` until a sync of its kind covers it or a job republishes
it. Once republished it is an ordinary job again, subject to the stream's 6
hour retention and to `MaxDeliver` like every push today.

## Consequences

- One sync per target in normal operation. Pushes during a sync collapse into
  one follow-up per kind.
- A namespace sync can wait up to one GitHub sync: 50 minutes during a
  bootstrap, seconds otherwise. Behind a GitHub sync that keeps failing, it
  waits for the retries too: up to the timeout cap, about 2.5 hours.
- A sync that keeps failing reaches its final attempt and the failure index
  instead of restarting under every push.
- The race packs stop accumulating. Existing leaked packs still need a full

They do still cost something, only on the GitHub side. Because the scope is `AllRefs`, git-sync asks GitHub for everything under `refs/`, so the GitHub ref list on every sync includes all `refs/pull/*/head` and `refs/pull/*/merge` refs. They're filtered out only after the whole list has arrived and been parsed. They don't affect the fetch's "have" lines, which come only from refs already on the mirror, and there are no PR refs there.

So on big repos with many PRs, the GitHub ref list may be much larger than the 20–65k refs that actually get compared. The pack stays the same size or close to it, because an updated ref's old value is the best base there is. A brand-new branch off the trunk is covered by the trunk tip. It doesn't need to be told. It works out which refs changed by comparing the two lists, and that comparison is the reason each sync lists all 50k refs on both sides.

**What one sync does now:**

1. **List GitHub's refs.** This gives every ref name and its commit (`newSession`, `internal/syncer/syncer.go:897`).
2. **List the mirror's refs**, the same way (`syncer.go:918`).
3. **Compare the two lists.** `BuildReplicationPlans` goes through them ref by ref (`internal/planner/planner.go:221`):
   - same commit on both sides: skip;
   - on GitHub only: create;
   - on both, different commit: update;
   - on the mirror only: delete (pruning).

   With 50k refs and one push, you get 49,999 skips and one update. Only the update goes on to the fetch (`classifyPlans`).
4. **Fetch from GitHub.** git-sync asks for the commits it's missing ("want") and lists what the mirror already has ("have"), so GitHub sends only the difference. This is the wasteful step: the "have" list is every ref tip on the mirror (`replicate.go:64` passes `p.TargetRefs`, and `fetch.go:251` sends all of them).
5. **Push the pack and the ref update to the mirror.**

**The change** is only in step 4. By then the plan already says which refs are being created or updated, and the "have" list can be built from that:

- **Updated ref:** send the mirror's current commit for that ref (`plan.TargetHash`). If `main` moved from A to B, saying "I have A" is enough for GitHub to send A..B. The other 49,999 tips add nothing, because GitHub only needs a commit on the path back from B to stop at.
- **New branch:** there's no old value, so send the mirror's default-branch tip (and maybe a few other likely bases). Most new branches start from the trunk.
- **Fallback:** for a large plan, such as many creates or a first sync, keep sending all tips. It's the safe choice, and the request size matters less there.

Roughly, for an update of `main` on a 50k-ref repo:

```
before: want B, have <50,000 tips>, done   (~3 MB request)
after:  want B, have A, have <trunk tip>, done   (~150 bytes)
```

**The trade-off** is that GitHub can only leave out what we tell it the mirror has. If a new branch shares history with some other branch but not the trunk, the smaller list misses that, and GitHub sends a larger pack than needed. The result is still correct, because the pack is complete. That's why the fallback threshold and a few extra bases matter, and why updates, which have an exact old value, are the safe case.

**What it doesn't fix:** steps 1–3 still list and compare 50k refs on both sides. To skip those, the job itself would have to carry the changed refs from the webhook, so git-sync could ask GitHub for just those names. That's a bigger change across fanout, the job format and git-sync, and the mirror side would still list everything.

- **Many branches at the same commit** (stale branches never moved off the trunk, release branches cut and left alone) collapse to one line each. Deduplication helps a lot here.
- **Tags** are almost always distinct, and annotated tags are sent as the tag object's own hash. A repo whose 50k refs are mostly tags still sends close to 50k lines.
- **Active feature branches** each have their own tip, so there's nothing to collapse.

All of the lines go in one request ending with "done", so there's no back-and-forth negotiation. The cost is one large request body, plus GitHub looking up each hash before it builds the pack.

For the 50k-ref repo you checked, the number of distinct hashes would tell you how much the "haves" change can save. `git ls-remote <url> | cut -f1 | sort -u | wc -l` against the mirror gives it (run it against GitHub, minus PR refs, if that's easier). If it's close to 50k, the change saves the full 3 MB per sync. If it's a few thousand, deduplication already takes care of most of it, and the time is going into the two ref listings.

content.text:
Yes. Every line of both ref lists is a commit hash plus a ref name, so the tips come back with the lists:

- **From GitHub:** git-sync's ref-listing request (protocol v2 `ls-refs`) asks for `peel` and `symrefs` (`internal/gitproto/refs.go:238`). Each ref arrives with its hash. Annotated tags also carry the commit they point to, and HEAD comes with the branch it points at.
- **From the mirror:** the older-protocol advertisement lists one `<hash> <refname>` line per ref, which git-sync reads in `AdvRefsToSlice` (`refs.go:181`). For an annotated tag, the hash is the tag object, not the commit.

Those hashes are everything git-sync uses:

- **Comparing:** the planner matches GitHub's hash and the mirror's hash for each ref name to decide skip, create, update or delete.
- **"Haves":** the fetch sends the mirror's hashes, deduplicated, back to GitHub.

So nothing extra needs to be fetched for the smaller "have" list. When `main` goes from A to B, both A (from the mirror list) and B (from the GitHub list) are already known before the fetch. The change only decides which of the hashes git-sync already holds go into the request: A and the trunk tip, rather than all ~50k.

What the lists don't contain is the commits between the tips, meaning the history. git-sync never stores that for a replicate sync: it streams the pack from GitHub straight to the mirror. That's why it can't work out the smallest set of "haves" on its own and has to choose by rule (old value of each updated ref, plus the trunk tip for new branches).
but if we get the list from right, the list from left then we could remove all the lines that are equal?

Mostly yes, and that's close to what I'm proposing. There's one exception that matters a lot.

If you drop every ref whose hash is the same on both sides (the skips), what remains on the mirror side is:

- **the old value of each updated ref.** That's the useful part: it's the commit the new tip builds on.
- **the value of each ref about to be deleted.** It's harmless, and could be dropped too.

For the common case, a push that moves `main` from A to B, that gives `want B, have A`, which is all GitHub needs.

The catch is that the unchanged refs are exactly the shared history. A "have" tells GitHub where it can stop walking back. If all of them are gone, GitHub has nowhere to stop, and in these cases it would send the whole history:

- **A new branch.** It has no old value, so after dropping the unchanged refs, the "have" list for it is empty. The branch was almost certainly cut from `main`, which didn't change, so `main`'s tip was dropped too. GitHub would send every commit reachable from the new branch: in effect a full clone, possibly gigabytes, close to the 10 GiB push ceiling.
- **A force push or rebase.** `feature` is rebased from A onto the current `main` and becomes B. A is no longer in B's history, so `have A` doesn't help. The real base, `main`'s tip, was dropped as unchanged, and the result is the same as above.
- **A merge.** `main` merges `release`. The old value of `main` covers one side. The `release` side is cut short only if `release`'s tip is in the list, and it was dropped as unchanged.

So the rule I'd use is "drop the equal lines, but keep a few of them":

- the mirror's old value of each updated ref;
- the default branch's tip, even when it didn't change, as the base for new branches and rebases;
- optionally, a small number of other tips (for example the most recently changed branches, or release branches) to cover merges;
- all tips, as today, when the plan is large.

The bad case can't break anything, only make one sync expensive. A "have" list that's too short makes the pack larger but never incorrect. It's still the reason the default-branch tip has to stay in the list even though its line is "equal".
yeah so the only issue would be multiple non common ancestor branches

Yes, with one refinement: it isn't all-or-nothing. Leaving out a base costs only the commits between the new tip and the nearest base still in the list. So:

- **A new branch cut from another feature branch** is fine. That branch's history is mostly on `main`, so the cost is the few extra commits of the parent branch, usually small.
- **A long-lived branch that split from `main` long ago** is the expensive case. Think of `release/1.x` maintained for years, or a fork-style branch. Pushing a new tag or branch from it would send everything since the split, which can be large.
- **A branch with no shared history at all**, like `gh-pages` or other orphan branches, means the full history of that branch.

There is a way to cover those cases without guessing. The protocol has negotiation rounds, and git-sync skips them today by always sending "done". Without "done":

1. **Round 1:** send the small list (old values of updated refs plus the default-branch tip) with no "done". GitHub replies with which of those commits it shares, and says "ready" once every wanted commit reaches one of them.
2. **If "ready":** GitHub sends the pack. This is the common case, and it's one request, as today, with a tiny body.
3. **If not:** send the remaining tips in the next round, or all of them as today, then "done". That costs one extra round trip, only in the diverged-branch case.

So GitHub's own reply decides whether the small list was enough, and the bad case falls back to today's behaviour instead of producing a huge pack. The extra work in git-sync is handling multiple rounds. Over HTTP each round is a new request that has to repeat the shared commits found so far, so it's a bit more code than just shortening the list.

I haven't checked one detail: exactly when GitHub declares "ready". Stock git checks that each wanted commit can reach a commit we listed. I'm not certain whether GitHub's server does the same, so it's worth testing against GitHub with a diverged branch before relying on it.

"""Send one protocol-v2 fetch round (no "done") and print the acknowledgments.

usage: negotiate.py URL want1[,want2] have1[,have2|-]
"""
import sys
import urllib.request


def pkt(s):
    b = s.encode() if isinstance(s, str) else s
    return b"%04x" % (len(b) + 4) + b


def read_pkts(data):
    i = 0
    while i < len(data):
        n = int(data[i:i + 4], 16)
        if n in (0, 1, 2):
            yield n, None
            i += 4
            continue
        yield n, data[i + 4:i + n]
        i += n


def main():
    url, wants, haves = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2].split(","), sys.argv[3]
    haves = [] if haves == "-" else haves.split(",")
    body = pkt("command=fetch\n") + pkt("agent=git-sync-probe\n") + pkt("object-format=sha1\n") + b"0001"
    body += pkt("ofs-delta\n") + pkt("no-progress\n")
    for w in wants:
        body += pkt(f"want {w}\n")
    for h in haves:
        body += pkt(f"have {h}\n")
    body += b"0000"
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url + "/git-upload-pack", data=body,
        headers={"Git-Protocol": "version=2", "Content-Type": "application/x-git-upload-pack-request",
                 "Accept": "application/x-git-upload-pack-result", "User-Agent": "git/2.47-git-sync-probe"})
    data = urllib.request.urlopen(req).read()
    acks, ready, sections = [], False, []
    for n, payload in read_pkts(data):
        if payload is None:
            continue
        line = payload.rstrip(b"\n")
        if line in (b"acknowledgments", b"packfile", b"shallow-info", b"wanted-refs"):
            sections.append(line.decode())
        elif line.startswith(b"ACK "):
            acks.append(line[4:].decode())
        elif line == b"NAK":
            acks.append("NAK")
        elif line == b"ready":
            ready = True
        if line == b"packfile":
            break
    print(f"request_bytes={len(body)} response_bytes={len(data)} sections={sections} ready={ready} acks={acks}")


main()

I've run the first test, sending raw fetch requests to GitHub against entireio/cli, and the results change the design. The script is at `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-soph--herdr-worktrees-git-sync-worktree-brave-forest-43d8/7915da1e-91f7-48c7-86de-a78b6561fbd0/scratchpad/negotiate.py`.

**Pack sizes, short "have" list versus every mirror tip:**

| Case | Short list | Every tip |
|---|---|---|
| New branch, cut from an older `main` | 32 KB | 32 KB |
| Orphan history (`refs/entire/checkpoints/...`) | 60 MB | 56 MB |
| Merge on `main` whose second parent is already on the mirror under another ref (a tag 110 commits ahead) | 1.39 MB | 113 KB |

(The plain-update numbers came out unfairly: other refs already contained `main`'s new tip, so the full list produced an empty pack. Those numbers aren't comparable.)

**Time spent on the "haves":**

| Haves sent | Request size | Time (3 runs each) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 213 B | ~0.65 s |
| 800 | 40 KB | ~0.55 s |
| 50,000 | 2.5 MB | ~2.2 s |

The 50k list was padded with random hashes that GitHub won't find, so real tips (found and walked) may cost more. These were timed from my machine, so the upload share will be smaller from us-east-2. That's roughly 1.5 s or more per sync on a 50k-ref repo, a real part of the 16 s p95 but not all of it. The two ref listings are the rest.

**What this changes:**

1. **The "ready" fallback doesn't work.** GitHub says "ready" only when the "have" is in the new tip's history. It didn't say it for the new branch, even though the short list gave the same pack as the full one. It did say it in the merge case, where the short list was 12× worse. So it rejects good cases and accepts bad ones. I'd drop negotiation rounds and keep the current single request with "done".
2. **The real risk is commits already on the mirror under another ref**, not orphan branches. Orphans are expensive either way. The common real form is merging a branch the mirror already has: GitHub resends that branch's commits. That's correct, just bigger, and capped at the size of the merged branch.
3. **Cheap improvements:** also send the tips of refs this sync deletes, since a merged branch is often deleted in the same push window. Keep the full list for large plans.

So the trade is about 1.5–2 s off every sync on 50k-ref repos, in exchange for occasionally larger packs when a merged branch was already mirrored. On the merge-heavy repos driving the queue, those packs could add up.

For building it, I'd turn these cases into a git-sync integration test using the `git-http-backend` fixtures the repo already has (`internal/syncer/git_http_backend_test.go`). The test would assert how many haves are sent and that the mirror ends up with exactly the same refs, for update, new branch, merge of a mirrored branch, and orphan.

Do you want the shorter list with that trade-off? The alternative is to first measure where the time goes in a real slow sync, in case the ref listings dominate.

content.text:
The slowdown isn't caused by ref counts. GitHub's git endpoints got slow for every repo, but only for requests from us-east-2, and they're still slow now (median about 5.3 s at 19:40).

**GitHub requests, last hour:**

| Requests | p50 | p95 |
|---|---|---|
| github.com `GET info/refs`, us-east-2 | 4.99 s | 6.60 s |
| github.com `GET info/refs`, all other regions | 0.25 s | 0.36 s |
| github.com `POST` (ref listing and fetch), us-east-2 | 5.30 s | 10.25 s |
| api.github.com (token minting), us-east-2 | 0.36 s | 0.46 s |

**Timeline, us-east-2 `GET info/refs` median:**

| Before 17:00 | 17:30 | 18:00 | 19:00 | 19:30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.10–0.17 s | 1.36 s | 3.93 s | 5.19 s | 5.51 s |

The upload-pack `POST`s follow the same curve, going from a 0.25 s median to 5.4 s.

**Why it isn't ref size:** in protocol v2, `GET info/refs` returns only GitHub's capability list, the same few hundred bytes for any repo, and it went from 0.1 s to 5 s. Small repos are as slow as big ones. The slowness is the same on all 25 pods, so it isn't one bad node. The mirror-side requests stayed fast (p95 0.08 s on the entry host).

**How it explains the incident:** each sync makes about 2.8 GitHub requests (one `GET`, then ref listing and usually a fetch as `POST`s). At about 5 s extra each, that adds roughly 14 s per sync, which matches the p95 going from 5 s to 16 s. Longer syncs on hot repos overlap more pushes, so deferrals went up. Throughput per pod dropped and the queue grew. Big repos show up as "most total sync work" because they get the most pushes, not because their ref counts changed.

**What's causing it is still open.** Only github.com, only from us-east-2, and api.github.com from the same region is fine. That points to either GitHub throttling our egress IPs (more likely if us-east-2 traffic from a few NAT IPs is heavy, and the 2–4× sync rate may have triggered it), or something on our egress path. The durations spread from 1 to 10 s rather than bunching at 5 s, so a DNS timeout is unlikely. Things worth checking:
- NAT gateway metrics for us-east-2 (`ErrorPortAllocation`, active connections, how many elastic IPs).
- Whether the time goes to connecting or waiting for GitHub's reply. Adding `otelhttptrace` to the worker's GitHub transport would split each span into DNS, connect, TLS and time to first byte, and would settle this next time.

On git-sync: before 17:00, a GitHub `POST` was 0.25 s at p50 and 3–6 s at p95. The "haves" change only affects part of that p95 on large repos, so it's a modest improvement and wouldn't have prevented this incident. I'd hold it until the GitHub latency is explained. One related change would help in exactly this situation: fewer GitHub round trips per sync. Each request now costs about 5 s, so going from 3 requests to 2 saves more than a smaller "have" list would.

These numbers come from sampled traces (about 1 in 3 syncs), so they're good for latencies and proportions, not totals.

The big "have" list only costs on the few repos with tens of thousands of distinct tips: about 1.5–2 s in my test against GitHub, and that test used random hashes, not real tips. The downside isn't limited to orphan branches either. Any merge of a branch the mirror already has would make GitHub resend that branch's commits, so the more common case would get worse in exchange for a small gain on a few repos.

If we revisit it, two things would be needed first:

- **Measurements on the big repos:** traces split into DNS, connect, TLS and time to first byte, to show how much of their `POST` time is really the "have" list.
- **A narrower rule:** keep the full list and only drop tips when a repo has more than, say, 10k distinct tips. That limits the risk to the repos where the saving is real.

content.text:
No. `ls-refs` has no option like that. The protocol v2 spec defines four arguments:

- `symrefs`: include where symbolic refs like HEAD point.
- `peel`: include the commit an annotated tag points to.
- `ref-prefix <prefix>`: only return refs under this name prefix (can be repeated).
- `unborn`: report HEAD even if it points at a branch with no commits yet.

All of them filter by name or add detail to a ref. None looks at history. GitHub's capability list for the cli repo confirms it supports nothing beyond the standard set:

```
version 2
agent=git/github-f6e509caf74d-Linux
ls-refs=unborn
fetch=shallow wait-for-done filter
server-option
object-format=sha1
```

`ls-refs=unborn` means only the optional `unborn` argument is offered. git-sync already sends it (`internal/gitproto/refs.go:245`) along with `peel`, `symrefs` and `ref-prefix`.

Returning only the tips that aren't in another ref's history would mean walking commit history on every listing, which is why ref listing never does it. Even if GitHub could, it would describe GitHub's history, and the "have" list has to describe the mirror's.

The mirror is the one place this could work, because entiredb is our server. A small endpoint (or a receive-pack extension) could return the mirror's tips minus any tip already contained in another tip's history. That's exactly the smallest correct "have" list, with no guessing and no merge-case penalty. entiredb would have to walk history to produce it, though, and the gain would be the same 1–2 s on a few repos. I'd only consider it if the trace measurements show the "have" list actually matters for the big repos.

content.text:
For cli the result is what you predicted for tags, and less so for branches:

| Namespace | Refs | Maximal tips |
|---|---|---|
| `refs/tags/` | 262 | 1 |
| `refs/heads/` | 518 | 448 |
| `refs/entire/` (checkpoints) | 59 | 59 |
| Total | 839 refs, 801 distinct | 508 |

Tags collapse to one. Branches barely shrink: most are unmerged feature branches, so each is its own tip. So how much this helps depends on the repo. A repo whose 50k refs are mostly tags would drop to a few hundred "haves". A repo with 50k live branches wouldn't shrink much.

**Can we find the maximal tips by negotiating with the mirror?** Not cheaply:

- **Acknowledgments don't help.** When the mirror acknowledges a "have", it only means "I have this object". It says nothing about whether one tip contains another, so one round can't tell us which tips are maximal.
- **Probing one tip at a time** works: "want T, have all the others", and an empty pack means T is contained. But that's one request per tip, tens of thousands for a big repo.
- **Fetching only commits from the mirror** (`filter tree:0`, which git-sync already uses in `FetchCommitParents`) and computing locally gives the full answer. It downloads the whole commit history on every sync, though, which costs more than the "have" list it saves.

**What would work is computing it inside entiredb.** The mirror already has the history locally. With commit-graph generation numbers, the equivalent of `merge-base --independent` is fast, and it updates cheaply on each push. When a ref moves to X, drop the maximal tips that X contains, and add X unless an existing tip contains it. entiredb would keep that set per repo and expose it, for example through a custom capability on the ref advertisement or a small endpoint. git-sync would then send that set as its "haves". The pack would be identical to today's, with no guessing and no merge-case penalty.

Whether it's worth building depends on what the big repos are made of. For the 50k-ref repo you looked at, this would give the split:

```
git ls-remote <url> | grep -v '\^{}' | grep -v refs/pull/ | awk '{print $2}' | cut -d/ -f1-2 | sort | uniq -c
```

Mostly `refs/tags` would make it a big win, since those collapse to a handful. Mostly `refs/heads` would make it a small one, and the 1–2 s from yesterday's estimate wouldn't move much.

- `v2/full/0000000000032`: 6 commits, 1 root commit.
- `v2/full/0000000000033`: 5 commits, 1 root commit.
- `v2/full/current`: 198 commits, 1 root commit.

`git merge-base` finds no common commit between any pair I tried. There are also 37 more `refs/entire/checkpoints/<XX>` refs besides the 21 under `v2/full`. Two things follow:

**1. They can't be shrunk away.** None of them contains another, so every one is a maximal tip. A maximal-tips list keeps all of them, which is why all 59 survived in cli. What can't be removed scales with the number of checkpoint refs. Each archived generation adds one, so that number keeps growing for repos that use Entire heavily.

**2. They still matter as "haves", even with no shared history.** GitHub leaves out every object reachable from a "have", including file contents and directory listings, not only commits. Generations `0032` and `0033` have no common commit but share 128 objects. That's why, in yesterday's test, the full list saved 4 MB (56 MB versus 60 MB) on a new checkpoint ref compared with sending only `main`'s tip. So sending only tips from the same history would make every new checkpoint generation more expensive.

For a "have" list this splits into two parts:

- **Code history (branches and tags):** maximal tips, computed in entiredb, would shrink it a lot on tag-heavy repos.
- **Checkpoint refs:** every one stays, unless we rely on our own layout. The format is ours, so a namespace rule is defensible. For a new or updated ref under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`, send `v2/full/current` and the most recent archived generation or two as "haves", not all of them. That's probably where nearly all the shared content is. It would need measuring, by comparing pack sizes for a new generation using all checkpoint tips versus only `current` plus the previous generation.

Both parts make the change bigger, and the gain on a healthy day is still small. I'd note this in the priority entry and keep the decision where we left it: measure on the big repos first. If those repos turn out to carry thousands of checkpoint refs, the namespace rule is the cheap first step, because it needs nothing from entiredb.

Yes, that one is safe, with one exception. Here's why, case by case:

- **A code branch or tag changes.** Its history shares nothing with the checkpoint histories: different commits, and in practice different files. Unchanged checkpoint tips can't make the pack smaller, so dropping them costs nothing.
- **An existing checkpoint ref is updated** (for example `v2/full/current` moves). The "have" that matters is that ref's own old value, which stays because it's a changed ref, not an equal one. New checkpoint commits add new session data that older generations won't contain, so the other checkpoint tips add next to nothing.
- **A new checkpoint ref is created** (a new archived generation). This is the exception. It has no old value, and its content overlaps with `current` and earlier generations. That overlap was the 4 MB in yesterday's test. For this case, keep the checkpoint tips, or at least `current` and the latest generations.

So the rule: unchanged checkpoint tips are left out of the "have" list unless the sync creates a checkpoint ref. Everything else stays as it is today, including every branch and tag tip. That keeps the full list exactly where it matters (branches and tags, which share history) and drops it only where there's nothing to share.

How I'd build it:

- **Generic in git-sync.** Neither git-sync nor the worker knows about `refs/entire/` today, and git-sync is a general library. I'd add a request option, something like `IndependentRefPrefixes`: "refs under these prefixes have histories independent of everything else". The "have" filter lives where the list is built (`fetchPackV2` and its callers in the replicate path). The worker passes `refs/entire/checkpoints/`.
- **Tests,** on the `git-http-backend` fixtures: a branch update with many unchanged checkpoint refs should send no checkpoint "haves" and give the same pack size as today; a new checkpoint generation should still send them; and the mirror's refs must match exactly in every case.

How much it saves is the number of checkpoint refs per repo: 59 of 801 tips in cli, so not much there. It only pays off if the big mirrors carry hundreds or thousands of checkpoint refs. A count from one of them would settle it:

```
git ls-remote <mirror-url> 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*' | wc -l
```

The risk is low and the change is small, so I'm happy to build it either way. Should I go ahead, or do you want to check that count first?

Without `v2/`, the checkpoint refs are fully independent, so the rule gets simpler:

- **Each ref is one checkpoint:** 37 refs, 1–4 commits each, each with its own root commit.
- **None contains another:** all 37 are maximal tips.
- **Almost nothing is shared:** of 411 objects across all of them, 17 appear under more than one ref (probably small identical files).

So the exception I proposed for new checkpoint refs isn't needed. A new checkpoint shares at most a handful of tiny objects with the existing ones, so leaving their tips out of the "have" list can't make its pack noticeably bigger.

The rule becomes: **for refs under the checkpoint prefix, send only the old value of a checkpoint ref being updated, and drop every unchanged one.** Branch and tag tips stay exactly as today. In the cases that matter:

| Sync changes | Checkpoint "haves" sent | Pack |
|---|---|---|
| A branch or tag | none | same as today |
| A new checkpoint ref | none | same, within a few small objects |
| An existing checkpoint ref | that ref's old value | same as today |

How much it saves is the number of checkpoint refs on a repo. That's only 37 on cli, but it grows by one per checkpoint, so for active Entire users it's the namespace that grows the "have" list fastest. Implementation as before: a generic option in git-sync (named for refs with independent histories, not for `refs/entire/`), which the worker sets to `refs/entire/checkpoints/`, with tests on the `git-http-backend` fixtures.

content.text:
`entireio/cli-checkpoints` is where they live, and it's the strongest case for the change.

**On GitHub:**

- 4,048 refs under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`: 4,026 checkpoints plus 22 under `v2/`. Apart from those there's only `refs/heads/entire` and HEAD.
- 4,049 distinct tips, so each sync of this repo sends about 4,050 "haves".
- The ref list alone is about 384 KB.

**Sample of 21 checkpoint refs, every 200th:**

- 1–3 commits each, each with its own root commit.
- All 21 are maximal tips.
- **0 shared objects** across 352 objects (about 27 MB in total).

So for this repo, the checkpoint rule cuts the "have" list from about 4,050 to the old value of whatever ref changed, usually none, because a new checkpoint is a new ref. Leaving those tips out can't make the pack bigger, since nothing is shared. Today's cost is moderate, about 200 KB of request body and probably a few hundred milliseconds at GitHub, going by yesterday's 50k-hash test. But it grows by one "have" per checkpoint, forever, and every customer repo that stores checkpoints the same way grows with it.

Two limits on what it fixes:

- **The ref listings still grow.** git-sync still lists all 4,000+ refs on both sides every sync, and that also grows with each checkpoint. Fixing that would need the changed refs in the job, or a different ref layout for checkpoints.
- **Pruning stays as it is.** The full ref lists are still compared, so deleted checkpoints are still pruned from the mirror. Only the fetch's "have" list changes.

The change itself is what I described before:

- **git-sync:** a generic request option for ref prefixes whose histories are independent. Under those prefixes, unchanged tips are left out of the "have" list and an updated ref keeps its own old value.
- **Worker:** sets the option to `refs/entire/checkpoints/`.
- **Tests,** on the `git-http-backend` fixtures, covering:
  - a branch update with many unchanged checkpoint refs (no checkpoint "haves", same pack);

func TestRun_GitHTTPBackendSync(t *testing.T) {
	if os.Getenv(gitHTTPBackendEnv) == "" {
		t.Skip("set GITSYNC_E2E_GIT_HTTP_BACKEND=1 to run git-http-backend integration test")
	}

	if _, err := exec.LookPath("git"); err != nil {
		t.Skipf("git not available: %v", err)
	}

	root := t.TempDir()
	sourceBare := filepath.Join(root, "source.git")
	targetBare := filepath.Join(root, "target.git")
	worktree := filepath.Join(root, "work")

	runGit(t, root, "init", "--bare", sourceBare)
	runGit(t, root, "init", "--bare", targetBare)
	runGit(t, targetBare, "config", "http.receivepack", "true")
	runGit(t, root, "init", "-b", testBranch, worktree)
	runGit(t, worktree, "config", "user.name", "git-sync test")
	runGit(t, worktree, "config", "user.email", "git-sync@example.com")

	writeFile(t, filepath.Join(worktree, "README.md"), "one\n")
	runGit(t, worktree, "add", "README.md")
	runGit(t, worktree, "commit", "-m", "initial")
	runGit(t, worktree, "remote", "add", "origin", sourceBare)
	runGit(t, worktree, "push", "origin", "HEAD:refs/heads/"+testBranch)

	server := newGitHTTPBackendServer(t, root)
	defer server.Close()

	sourceURL := server.RepoURL("source.git")
	targetURL := server.RepoURL("target.git")

	result, err := Run(context.Background(), Config{
		Source: Endpoint{URL: sourceURL},
		Target: Endpoint{URL: targetURL},
	})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("initial sync failed: %v", err)
	}
	if result.Pushed != 1 || result.Blocked != 0 {
		t.Fatalf("unexpected initial result: %+v", result)
	}
	if !result.Relay || result.RelayMode != relayModeBootstrap {
		t.Fatalf("expected initial empty-target sync to use bootstrap relay, got %+v", result)
	}

	assertGitRefEqual(t, sourceBare, targetBare, plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(testBranch))

	writeFile(t, filepath.Join(worktree, "README.md"), "one\ntwo\n")
	runGit(t, worktree, "add", "README.md")
	runGit(t, worktree, "commit", "-m", "second")
	runGit(t, worktree, "push", "origin", "HEAD:refs/heads/"+testBranch)

	result, err = Run(context.Background(), Config{
		Source: Endpoint{URL: sourceURL},
		Target: Endpoint{URL: targetURL},
	})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("incremental sync failed: %v", err)
	}
	if result.Pushed != 1 || result.Blocked != 0 {
		t.Fatalf("unexpected incremental result: %+v", result)
	}
	if !result.Relay || result.RelayMode != relayModeIncremental {
		t.Fatalf("expected incremental sync to use incremental relay, got %+v", result)
	}

	assertGitRefEqual(t, sourceBare, targetBare, plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(testBranch))
}

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Fixed

- **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A push the target refused or timed out, and resume markers left on the target, go at Warn; a push git-sync stops itself at its byte budget and then splits stays at Info, so a successful bootstrap logs no warnings. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows every line it showed before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))
- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.
- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.
- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.
- SSH fetches from GitHub intermittently failed with `update object storage: empty packfile`. The SSH transport wrote the request and closed stdin while the server was still streaming its ref advertisement (36 MB for `NixOS/nixpkgs`), and GitHub sometimes dropped a request that arrived that early. The request is now sent only after the advertisement is read, which is what `git` does. On the old code, 2 of 4 runs against `git@github.com:NixOS/nixpkgs.git` failed; with the change, 7 of 7 passed.
- Errors from closing an upload-pack stream (the ssh exit status and the remote's stderr) were dropped in `fetchToStoreV1` and `fetchToStoreV2`, because `CheckClose` wrote to a shadowed `err`. They are now joined into the returned error.

## [0.10.0] - 2026-10-21

### Security

- Bumped the Go toolchain to `1.27.3` (go.mod `toolchain` and the mise pin), clearing GO-2026-6809: `crypto/x509` now distrusts compromised intermediate certificates. It is reachable through TLS verification on every HTTPS remote. ([#126](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/126))

- Bumped the Go toolchain to `1.27.2` (go.mod `toolchain` and the mise pin), clearing ten standard-library advisories reachable from the HTTP transport and the `convert-sha256` filesystem paths — among them HTTP/1 client desynchronization after a `CONNECT` rejection (GO-2026-6605), a memory-limit bypass parsing MIME headers in `net/textproto` (GO-2026-6608), malformed ECH outer extension references accepted by `crypto/tls` (GO-2026-6607), and HTTP/2 transport accepting malformed framing headers (GO-2026-6610). Released binaries are built from the go.mod toolchain; `govulncheck ./...` goes from 10 called vulnerabilities to 0. The `go` directive stays at `1.26`, so the minimum Go version for library consumers is unchanged. golangci-lint moves to `v2.15.0`, since releases before `v2.13.0` refuse to lint a module targeting Go 1.27. ([#125](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/125))

- Bumped `golang.org/x/crypto` to `v0.58.0` and `golang.org/x/net` to `v0.61.0` (raised as indirect dependencies; `golang.org/x/sys` follows to `v0.49.0`), clearing three SSH advisories in packages git-sync imports (GO-2026-6303, GO-2026-6354, GO-2026-6355) and five HTTP/2 advisories in `golang.org/x/net`. None was reachable from git-sync's call graph. The remaining module-level finding, GO-2026-5932 (`golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp` is unmaintained), has no fix and git-sync does not import that package. ([#125](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/125))

I've built the change in git-sync. It's not committed yet. The race-detector suite, the git-http-backend tests and the linter all pass.

**What it does:** there's a new request option, `RefScope.IndependentHistoryRefPrefixes`. Under those prefixes, a fetch from GitHub no longer offers the mirror's unchanged tips as "haves". A ref the run updates is still offered, as its own old value. Which refs get synced or pruned doesn't change, and with the option empty, behaviour is exactly as before.

**Where it applies:** the replicate path, which is what the worker uses, and sync mode's incremental relay. Two other fetches still send every tip:
- **Sync mode's earlier fetch:** before planning, sync mode fetches history to check fast-forwards. No plan exists yet at that point, and that check is the wrong place to experiment.
- **Bootstrap:** first syncs and batched retries.

**Code changes:**
- `internal/planner/haves.go`: `FetchHaves` decides which mirror tips are offered.
- `internal/syncer/syncer.go`: `executeReplicate` and `executeIncremental` use it, and the session validates the prefixes.
- `types.go`, `client.go`, `unstable/client.go`: the new field is documented, validated (it must start with `refs/`) and passed through every config builder, as the existing guard test requires.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: an entry under Unreleased.

**Tests:**
- **Unit tests** for the "have" rule and for validation.
- **Integration tests** (`internal/syncer/independent_history_test.go`), each on a source with a branch and three checkpoint refs. Every test records the exact "have" lines each fetch sent and checks that the mirror's refs match the source exactly:

| Scenario | Haves sent |
|---|---|
| Branch update | the branch's old value only |
| Branch update, option off | the branch plus all 3 checkpoint tips (today's behaviour) |
| New checkpoint ref | the branch tip only |
| Update to an existing checkpoint ref | the branch tip plus that ref's old value |
| Sync mode | first fetch: everything; relay fetch: the branch's old value |
| Checkpoint deleted on the source | no fetch at all; the mirror drops the ref |

**Still to do:**
1. Commit this and open a git-sync PR. Say if you want me to.
2. Once a git-sync version with this is available, the worker change in mirror-pipeline: bump the pin and set `IndependentHistoryRefPrefixes: []string{"refs/entire/checkpoints/"}` in `refScopeFor`.
3. Deleting the 22 `v2/` refs in entireio/cli and entireio/cli-checkpoints, if you want that done. I haven't touched them.

---

**Title:** relay: leave unchanged independent-history tips out of the haves

A relay fetch offers the source every target tip as a have. For refs that each carry their own history, such as one orphan history per session checkpoint, those tips cannot shorten the pack the run needs. A repository with about 4,000 checkpoint refs sends about 4,000 have lines on a run that moved one branch, and the count grows by one per checkpoint.

This adds `RefScope.IndependentHistoryRefPrefixes`. Under those prefixes, a target ref is offered as a have only when the run updates it, as its own old value. Every other target tip is offered as before. Which refs are synced or pruned does not change, and with the option empty the behaviour is identical to today.

Where it applies:
- Replicate relays and sync's incremental relay.
- Not sync's closure fetch for fast-forward checks, which runs before any plan exists, and not bootstrap. Both still offer every tip.

Why it's safe: in a sample of 21 checkpoint refs from a real checkpoint repository, each had 1–3 commits and its own root, and none shared an object with another. So leaving their unchanged tips out cannot make a pack larger by more than a few small identical objects.

- Unit tests for `planner.FetchHaves` and for prefix validation.
- In-process integration tests that record the have lines of every source fetch and check that the target's refs match the source exactly. They cover a branch update (with the option and as a baseline without it), a new checkpoint ref, an update to an existing checkpoint ref, sync mode's two fetches, and a prune-only run (no fetch).

content.text:
I addressed all four review points, pushed them as commit `601350fa`, and updated the trail description to match: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2748

1. **Tests where the named refs share history.** Two new integration tests configure the prefix over refs that are not independent:
   - a new ref under the prefix built on an existing one;
   - a branch moved onto a commit the mirror holds only under the prefix.

   Both leave a complete copy; the source just resends some objects. The shared check (`assertSameRefs`) now reads every commit, tree and blob reachable from each mirror ref, not only the tips, so the six earlier tests check the full history too. I didn't confirm that the deeper check actually fails on a broken copy, by removing an object on purpose.
2. **How prefixes match** (`types.go`): the doc now says each entry is a literal string prefix of the mirror's ref names (after `Mappings`), with no globs. It also says to end a namespace with a slash, for example `refs/entire/checkpoints/`, because otherwise it also matches `refs/entire/checkpoints-old`.
3. **"Never wrong, only costly"** is qualified. Naming refs that share history keeps the copy correct, but the larger pack can exceed a pack size limit (`unstable`'s `MaxPackBytes`) or a server's request limit. So a transfer that worked without the option can fail with it. The CHANGELOG entry says the same.
4. **Validator doc** (`validation.go`): it now says what the check enforces (each entry, once trimmed, starts with `refs/`) and what it doesn't. Something like `refs/foo*` passes and only matches names that literally contain `*`.

content.text:
I fixed the test weakness and pushed it as commit `e7f85951` to PR #138 (https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/138). The reviewer's diagnosis was right: in the pinned go-git (v6.0.0-alpha.5), `TreeWalker.Next` turns a failed subtree lookup into `io.EOF` (`plumbing/object/tree.go:704-706`). So the old check stopped early on a missing subdirectory and reported success.

- **Explicit walk:** `assertClosureReadable` now calls a new `readClosure`. It follows parent commits and tree entries itself and reads every commit, tree and blob, failing as soon as one is missing. An unexpected file mode is reported as an error instead of being skipped.
- **Nested fixture:** checkpoint commits now have a `0/` directory next to `metadata.json`, like real checkpoints. Every integration test therefore checks a subdirectory.
- **Missing objects are caught:** the new `TestReadClosureDetectsMissingObjects` removes a subtree, a blob inside the subdirectory, and a parent commit, one at a time. Each time, `readClosure` has to name the missing object, and it does. In the subtree case, go-git's own iterator still reported success when the subtree was gone.

The race-detector run of the syncer tests, the git-http-backend tests and the linter all pass. The full race-detector suite last ran on the commit before this one; the only file changed since is this test file. The PR description still holds, so I didn't change it.

## Summary

- Bumps `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` from alpha to `v6.0.0-beta.1`.
- Bumps `testify` to `v1.12.1` and the indirect dependencies: `golang.org/x/net` `v0.62.0`, `golang.org/x/sync` `v0.24.0`, `ProtonMail/go-crypto` `v1.5.2`, `cloudflare/circl` `v1.6.5`, `pjbgf/sha1cd` `v0.7.0`, `Microsoft/go-winio` `v0.6.4`, `spf13/pflag` `v1.0.10`. `go mod tidy` drops a few indirect entries that are no longer needed.
- The Go toolchain stays at `1.27.3`, which is the current release.

## Behavior change: refs starting with a dash are now mirrored

go-git beta.1 removed the leading-dash rule from `ReferenceName.Validate`. Git applies that rule only when a branch or tag is created (`check_branch_ref` / `check_tag_ref`), not in `check_refname_format`, and `git fetch` and `git clone` replicate `refs/heads/-foo` without complaint. `PartitionRefNames` and `--map` validation both defer to `Validate`, so such refs are now mirrored instead of skipped.

The rejection was never a deliberate git-sync choice. 0f6a015e adopted `Validate` to block path traversal and NUL injection, and the dash rule came along with it. That commit's stated goal was to match git and skip nothing git accepts, which this restores. No ref name reaches a command line in a position where a leading dash would be read as an option. The only place one is passed to a subprocess is `git tag -s converted/<short> refs/heads/<short>` in `sha256convert`.

The test case moves from `TestPartitionRefNamesRejectsDangerousNames` to `TestPartitionRefNamesKeepsLegitimateNames`, and the doc comment on `PartitionRefNames` is updated to match.

S=/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-soph--herdr-worktrees-git-sync-worktree-brave-forest-43d8/7915da1e-91f7-48c7-86de-a78b6561fbd0/scratchpad; A=$HOME/go/pkg/mod/github.com/go-git/go-git/v6@v6.0.0-alpha.5; B=$HOME/go/pkg/mod/github.com/go-git/go-git/v6@v6.0.0-beta.1; python3 -I - "$A" "$B" "$S/used.txt" <<'EOF' > $S/gogit-changed.txt
import sys,os,difflib
A,B,U=sys.argv[1:4]
root='github.com/go-git/go-git/v6'
for p in open(U).read().split():
    d=p[len(root):].lstrip('/')
    da,db=os.path.join(A,d),os.path.join(B,d)
    ls=lambda x: set(f for f in os.listdir(x) if f.endswith('.go') and not f.endswith('_test.go')) if os.path.isdir(x) else set()
    fa,fb=ls(da),ls(db)
    for f in sorted(fa|fb):
        name=(d+'/' if d else '')+f
        if f not in fb: print('REMOVED', name); continue
        if f not in fa: print('ADDED', name); continue
        a=open(os.path.join(da,f)).read().splitlines(); b=open(os.path.join(db,f)).read().splitlines()
        if a!=b:
            n=sum(1 for l in difflib.unified_diff(a,b,lineterm='',n=0) if l[:1] in '+-' and not l.startswith(('+++','---')))
            print(n, name)
EOF
grep -v -E "worktree|status.go|submodule|gitignore|merkletrie|crypto.go|sshagent|knownhosts" $S/gogit-changed.txt | sort -k1 -rn | head -50

## Problem

Two syncs running at the same time can undo each other's work. git-sync used to read source refs and then target refs. If another sync finished between those two reads, its newer target state became our expected-old value. The lease check then passed, and we pushed an older source snapshot over it, rewinding a branch or pruning a ref the other sync had just created.

## Changes

- **Read target refs before source refs.** The expected-old snapshot can then never be newer than the source snapshot pushed over it.
- **Count work another sync already did as skipped.** A rejection can mean another writer moved the ref. These messages count: `remote ref has changed`, `stale info` and `already exists`, plus stock Git's `incorrect old value provided` and `failed to update ref`. On one of these, git-sync re-reads the target. If the ref already holds exactly the desired hash, it counts as skipped instead of failing. No write is retried. Deletes, policy refusals and a different hash still fail.
- **Drain receive-pack before the re-read, and only then.** Hook output after the report then can't break SSH or helper processes before the re-read. The drain is capped at 1 MiB. Every other push closes right away as before, so an early refusal such as a body limit still stops the upload, and teardown errors are still ignored, because the report already says what was committed. If the drain or the re-read fails, the rejection stands with a warning.

## Examples

1. **Rewind prevented:** A reads source `main=X`. B then syncs `main=Y` and a new `feature`. A no longer pushes `Y → X` or deletes `feature`.
2. **Newer update kept:** A pushes `X → Y`, but B has already installed `Z`. The re-read sees `Z`, so A fails and `Z` stays.
3. **Already done:** A pushes `X → Y`, and B has already installed `Y`. A succeeds, with the ref counted as skipped.

## Tradeoffs

- The target is now contacted first, so its auth prompts or failures come before the source's. This is documented in `docs/usage.md`.
- This doesn't serialize concurrent runs, and it doesn't detect a ref that moved away and back to the same hash.

## Testing

- Deterministic interleaving tests cover the replicate, sync, materialized, bootstrap and best-effort paths. The regression tests fail without the fix.
- Unit tests cover:
  - recognizing the rejection messages;
  - hidden or absent refs;
  - mixed rejections and split batches;
  - trailing sideband output on SSH and helper transports;
  - transport errors and oversized output after the report;
  - early unpack refusals closing without a drain.
- `go test -race ./...` and `mise run lint` pass.

18-- **`RefScope.IndependentHistoryRefPrefixes` shrinks the haves of a relay fetch.** A relay fetch offers the source every target tip as a have. For refs that each carry their own history, such as one orphan history per session checkpoint, those tips cannot shorten the pack, and a repository with thousands of them sent thousands of have lines for a run that changed one branch. Under the named prefixes, a target ref is now offered only when the run updates it, as its own old value. Replicate and sync's incremental relay honor it. Sync's closure fetch for fast-forward checks and bootstrap still offer every tip. Which refs are synced or pruned does not change. Every entry must start with `refs/`.

21-### Fixed

23-- **A branch whose new tip the target already holds under another ref now fast-forwards instead of failing the sync.** The planning fetch names every target ref as a have, so the source prunes such a tip from the pack and the ancestry check aborted the run with `load source commit …: object not found`. A mirror of NixOS/nixpkgs hit this whenever `nixos-unstable` advanced to a commit `master` had already delivered. A check the pruned store cannot settle is now resolved with one tree:0 commit-graph fetch of that tip against the ref's own target hash: a real fast-forward updates, and a rewind blocks as `not an ancestor`. A source that cannot serve that fetch (protocol v1, no filter support) leaves the ref blocked with the reason instead of crashing. Builds on [#79](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/79).
24-- **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A push the target refused or timed out, and resume markers left on the target, go at Warn; a push git-sync stops itself at its byte budget and then splits stays at Info, so a successful bootstrap logs no warnings. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows every line it showed before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))
25-- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.
26-- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.
27-- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.

input.content:
`TreeWalker.Next` turns a failed subtree lookup into `io.EOF`, so a recursive walk over a tree with a missing subtree ends early and reports success. `Tree.Files().ForEach` and anything else built on `FileIter` returns `nil` for an incomplete tree, and every entry after the missing subtree is silently dropped, not only the subtree's own contents.

The code is in `plumbing/object/tree.go` (lines 704-706 in `v6.0.0-beta.1`, 726-728 on `main` at ae4b49cdd0; the same in `v6.0.0-alpha.5`):

```go
if entry.Mode == filemode.Dir {
	obj, err = GetTree(w.s, entry.Hash)
}

name = simpleJoin(w.base, entry.Name)

if err != nil {
	err = io.EOF
	return name, entry, err
}
```

The doc comment on `Next` says objects that cannot be found "will be skipped automatically", but the walk does not skip the entry, it stops. Any `GetTree` error is mapped to `io.EOF`, not only `plumbing.ErrObjectNotFound`, so a decode or storage error also reads as a clean end of iteration.

### Reproduction

A root tree with `a.txt`, `dir/inner.txt` and `z.txt`, with the `dir` tree object removed from a `memory.Storage`:

```go
s := memory.NewStorage()
sub := store(s, &object.Tree{Entries: []object.TreeEntry{{Name: "inner.txt", Mode: filemode.Regular, Hash: blob(s, "inner")}}})
rh := store(s, &object.Tree{Entries: []object.TreeEntry{
	{Name: "a.txt", Mode: filemode.Regular, Hash: blob(s, "a")},
	{Name: "dir", Mode: filemode.Dir, Hash: sub},
	{Name: "z.txt", Mode: filemode.Regular, Hash: blob(s, "z")},
}})
delete(s.ObjectStorage.Objects, sub)
delete(s.ObjectStorage.Trees, sub)

t, _ := object.GetTree(s, rh)
var seen []string
err := t.Files().ForEach(func(f *object.File) error { seen = append(seen, f.Name); return nil })
fmt.Println(seen, err)
```

Output on `v6.0.0-beta.1`:

```
[a.txt] <nil>
```

Expected: an error that wraps `plumbing.ErrObjectNotFound` and names the missing tree. At the least, `z.txt` should still be visited if skipping stays the documented behaviour.

### Impact

Callers that use `Files()` or `TreeWalker` to check that a tree is complete (after a fetch, a partial clone, or a pack import) get a false pass. We hit this in a test helper meant to prove every object reachable from a ref was readable. It kept passing with a subtree deleted from storage, so we replaced it with an explicit walk.

### Suggested fix

Return the `GetTree` error from `Next` instead of `io.EOF`, and update the doc comment. Callers that relied on the skip behaviour would see an error where they saw a short walk, so this may want a mention in the v6 release notes. If the skip is meant to stay, `Next` should skip that one entry and continue with its siblings, and only `plumbing.ErrObjectNotFound` should be skipped.

content.text:
I checked how git-sync uses go-git's tree walker. My recommendation is not to move to go-git `main` for this fix: git-sync doesn't need it, and pinning an untagged commit has a cost.

- **No git-sync code hits the bug.** Only one non-test place reads trees, the object collector at `internal/planner/planner.go:814`. It reads `tree.Entries` itself and returns an error when a lookup fails. Nothing outside tests calls `TreeWalker`, `Files()`, `DiffTree` or merkletrie, which is the code the fix (go-git #2556) changes.
- **The tests already cover it.** The only `Files().ForEach` call is in the regression test at `internal/syncer/independent_history_test.go:498`. The real check there is `readClosure`, which works on either version. That line just logs a note once go-git reports the missing subtree.
- **The cost:** go-git `main` is 89 commits ahead of `v6.0.0-beta.1`, and nothing newer has been tagged. A public library pinned to an unreleased commit takes on all 89 untested changes for its consumers, including the mirror-pipeline bump that's coming.

I'd stay on `beta.1` and move when go-git tags the next release (beta.2 or whatever it is called). At that point the test's log note should start appearing, and the explicit walk can stay as a stricter check or be simplified.

If you want to try `main` early anyway, I can run `go get github.com/go-git/go-git/v6@main` on a branch and run the race test suite. It won't change behaviour for the reasons above.

Large receive-pack requests always advertise `Content-Length`, allowing

efb64e63dc plumbing: object, Decode tree modes of any length

Git accepts any nonempty run of octal digits as a tree entry mode, so
it reads a tree written with a zero-padded mode such as
`00000000000100644`, or with a mode wider than 32 bits such as
`1000000100644`, and `git ls-tree` prints `100644` for both. go-git
refused any mode longer than 7 digits, so it could not read such a
tree at all, and a mode longer than its 4096-byte read buffer failed
with a bare `bufio.ErrBufferFull` rather than `ErrMalformedTree`.

`Tree.Decode` now reads a mode of any length, in chunks and in
constant memory, and keeps the low 32 bits of a wider value. Git keeps
the low 16, and the bits that decide the mode are in both. Every
malformed mode, whatever its length, fails with `ErrMalformedTree`.

`filemode.FromBytes` accepts input longer than 7 digits too, but stays
strict about range: like `filemode.New`, it returns an error for a
value wider than 32 bits. Nothing that parsed before parses to a
different value. The text of its errors changed, and it reports an
empty mode as "empty mode".

Tried it: moving to go-git `main` works and changes nothing you'd notice. I'd still wait for the next go-git tag before shipping it.

**What I did:** made a local branch `soph/go-git-main` off `main` with one commit that moves go-git and go-billy to their latest `main` commits. Nothing else in `go.mod` changed, and nothing is pushed.

**Results:**
- Build, `go vet`, the full race test suite, `mise run lint` and the git-http-backend suite all pass.
- The go-git fix is confirmed. The `Files().ForEach` call in the regression test now returns `object not found` for the deleted subtree, and the test logs that the workaround is no longer needed.

**What else comes with it:** go-git `main` is 89 commits past `beta.1`. From the commit titles, the ones in code git-sync uses:
- **Stricter pack parsing.** go-git now rejects truncated packs and objects shorter than their declared size. That turns bad input into clear errors, and our tests don't hit it.
- **HTTP push framing.** Large pushes now go out without a `Content-Length`, as git does. This doesn't reach git-sync: it builds its own HTTP requests in `internal/gitproto/smarthttp.go`.
- **Tree entry modes, in `convert-sha256`.** This is the only real behaviour change. go-git now reads tree entry modes the way git does, and `convert-sha256` decodes and re-encodes every tree.
  - A file with an execute bit set but not the owner's, such as `100011`, used to be written as `100755` and is now written as `100644`.
  - Trees with zero-padded modes, which used to fail to decode, now convert.
  - So for those rare trees, the SHA-256 hash changes between git-sync versions. The tests have no such trees.
  - The conversion already didn't copy modes byte for byte, so this widens an existing difference rather than adding a new one.

**Recommendation:** keep the branch as a preview, and bump when go-git tags beta.2 or whatever comes next. At that point we can drop the `Files().ForEach` note from the test and mention the `convert-sha256` mode change in the CHANGELOG. Shipping now would pin a public library to an untagged commit and gain nothing, since no git-sync code uses the fixed walker.

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- **`RefScope.IndependentHistoryRefPrefixes` shrinks the haves of a relay fetch.** A relay fetch offers the source every target tip as a have. For refs that each carry their own history, such as one orphan history per session checkpoint, those tips cannot shorten the pack, and a repository with thousands of them sent thousands of have lines for a run that changed one branch. Under the named prefixes, a target ref is now offered only when the run updates it, as its own old value. Replicate and sync's incremental relay honor it. Sync's closure fetch for fast-forward checks and bootstrap still offer every tip. Which refs are synced or pruned does not change. Entries are literal prefixes of target ref names and must start with `refs/`; end a namespace with a slash. Naming refs that do share history keeps the copy complete but resends objects the target already holds, and the larger pack can hit a pack or request size limit.

### Changed

- Bumped `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` to `v6.0.0-beta.1`, along with `testify` `v1.12.1` and the indirect dependencies (`golang.org/x/net` `v0.62.0`, `golang.org/x/sync` `v0.24.0`, `ProtonMail/go-crypto` `v1.5.2`, `cloudflare/circl` `v1.6.5`, `pjbgf/sha1cd` `v0.7.0`, `Microsoft/go-winio` `v0.6.4`, `spf13/pflag` `v1.0.10`). The Go toolchain stays at `1.27.3`, the current release.
- Refs whose name starts with a dash (`refs/heads/-foo`) are now mirrored instead of skipped. go-git `beta.1` dropped that rule from `ReferenceName.Validate` to match git's `check_refname_format`: git restricts a leading dash only when a branch or tag is created, and `git fetch` and `git clone` replicate such refs. `--map` accepts such names for the same reason. No ref name reaches a command line where a leading dash would be read as an option.

Moves `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` from `v6.0.0-beta.1` to their `main` commits of 4 November 2026 (`bbee1d214130` and `3dcdd520bf27`), ahead of the next tagged release. No other module changes.

The reason is [go-git/go-git#2555](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/2555): `TreeWalker.Next` turned a subtree it could not read into `io.EOF`, so `Tree.Files().ForEach` returned `nil` for an incomplete tree and dropped every entry after the gap. go-git main returns the lookup error instead. No git-sync code outside tests walks trees with it, so this changes no sync behaviour. The closure regression test now requires the error, and its comments no longer describe the old behaviour.

Other changes in the 89 go-git commits that reach git-sync:
- Packs cut off in the header, or with objects shorter than their declared size, are rejected with an error.
- `convert-sha256` decodes tree entry modes as git does. A regular file whose mode has an execute bit set but not the owner's, such as `100011`, now converts as `100644` instead of `100755`, so such a tree gets a different SHA-256 hash than an earlier version produced. A tree with a zero-padded mode, which failed to decode, now converts. No test fixture has such a tree.
- Large HTTP pushes in go-git no longer send `Content-Length`. git-sync builds its own HTTP requests in `internal/gitproto`, so its pushes are unchanged.

Tradeoff: git-sync pins untagged go-git commits until the next release. The bump can move to that tag once it exists.

Tests: `go test -race ./...`, the git-http-backend suite and `mise run lint` pass.

Moves `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` from `v6.0.0-beta.1` to their `main` commits of 4 November 2026 (`bbee1d214130` and `3dcdd520bf27`), ahead of the next tagged release. No other module changes.

The reason is [go-git/go-git#2555](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/2555): `TreeWalker.Next` turned a subtree it could not read into `io.EOF`, so `Tree.Files().ForEach` returned `nil` for an incomplete tree and dropped every entry after the gap. go-git main returns the lookup error instead. No git-sync code outside tests walks trees with it, so this changes no sync behaviour. The closure regression test now requires the error, and its comments no longer describe the old behaviour.

Other changes in the 89 go-git commits that reach git-sync:
- Packs cut off in the header, or with objects shorter than their declared size, are rejected with an error.
- `convert-sha256` decodes tree entry modes as git does. A regular file whose mode has an execute bit set but not the owner's, such as `100011`, now converts as `100644` instead of `100755`, so such a tree gets a different SHA-256 hash than an earlier version produced. A tree with a zero-padded mode, which failed to decode, now converts. No test fixture has such a tree.
- Large HTTP pushes in go-git no longer send `Content-Length`. git-sync builds its own HTTP requests in `internal/gitproto`, so its pushes are unchanged.

Tradeoff: git-sync pins untagged go-git commits until the next release. The bump can move to that tag once it exists.

Tests: `go test -race ./...`, the git-http-backend suite and `mise run lint` pass.

I bumped go-git and go-billy to their latest `main` and opened the trail:
https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2763/changes/git-sync/10

The branch `soph/go-git-main` is pushed as one commit, `3e978daa`. It contains:
- **The bump.** `go.mod` and `go.sum` now point at go-git `bbee1d214130` and go-billy `3dcdd520bf27`; no other module moved.
- **The test.** The missing-subtree regression test now fails unless go-git's `Files().ForEach` reports the missing subtree as an error. Before, it only logged a note. The comments no longer describe the old go-git behaviour.
- **The CHANGELOG.** A `### Changed` entry links go-git/go-git#2555 and covers the stricter pack checks. It also covers the `convert-sha256` tree-mode change: a file mode like `100011` now converts as `100644` instead of `100755`, so such a tree gets a different SHA-256 hash.

The full race test suite, `mise run lint` and the git-http-backend suite all pass. The trail description says git-sync now pins untagged go-git commits until go-git tags its next release.
should we not just remove the comments? like why keep comments explaining that something was broken but is now fixed?

You're right. Those comments are history, and the commit message and CHANGELOG already cover it. The `Files().ForEach` assertion goes too: it tests go-git rather than git-sync, and its only justification was the comment. `readClosure` still checks that a missing subtree is reported.

I removed both comments, along with the `Files().ForEach` check that existed only to show the old go-git behaviour. Compared with `main`, the test file now only loses lines:
- The `Files().ForEach` probe and its comment are gone from the missing-subtree test. The test still requires `readClosure` to name the missing subtree.
- The `readClosure` doc comment now just says what the function does: it walks parents and tree entries, reports a missing object as an error, and reads every blob.

The syncer tests (with the race detector) and lint pass. The change isn't committed yet.

Two other places still say the test "now requires that error", and that's no longer true: the pushed commit message, and the sentence in the trail description. I'd amend the commit, update that sentence, and `git push --force-with-lease`. The branch has one commit and was only just pushed. Should I go ahead?
